claim: Four novel Cre-inducible (LSL) Kras alleles were generated in mice with the biochemically distinct G12D or Q61R mutations encoded by native (nat) rare or common (com) codons to produce low or high protein levels.
source: To attempt to separate these two effects, we generated four novel Cre-inducible (LSL) Kras alleles in mice with the biochemically distinct G12D or Q61R mutations and encoded by native (nat) rare or common (com) codons to produce low or high protein levels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the generation of four novel alleles as part of the experimental design.

claim: Each of the four Kras alleles induced a distinct transcriptional response shortly after activation in vivo.
source: While there were similarities, each allele also induced a distinct transcriptional response shortly after activation in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced transcriptional hallmarks suggestive of an expansion of multipotent cells.
source: At one end of the spectrum, activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced transcriptional hallmarks suggestive of an expansion of multipotent cells
evidence: This claim is based on transcriptome analysis and GSEA hallmarks presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele led to hallmarks of hyperproliferation and oncogenic stress.
source: while at the other end, activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele led to hallmarks of hyperproliferation and oncogenic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis and GSEA hallmarks data.

claim: Hematolymphopoietic lesions were permissive to the level of active oncoprotein.
source: revealing that hematolymphopoietic lesions were permissive to the level of active oncoprotein
evidence: This is based on tumorigenesis studies where all four alleles were globally activated.

claim: Squamous tumors were permissive to the G12D mutant.
source: squamous tumors were permissive to the G12D mutant
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis of forestomach and oral tumors in the global activation study.

claim: Carcinomas were permissive to both the level of active oncoprotein and the G12D mutation.
source: while carcinomas were permissive to both these features.
evidence: This is based on lung tumor analysis in the global activation study.

claim: Different KRAS mutations impart unique signaling properties that are preferentially capable of inducing tumor initiation in a distinct cell-specific manner.
source: We suggest that different KRAS mutations impart unique signaling properties that are preferentially capable of inducing tumor initiation in a distinct cell-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data of transcriptome analysis and tumorigenesis studies.

claim: KRAS is the most commonly mutated of the RAS family (KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS).
source: Focusing on KRAS, the most commonly mutated of the three (Prior et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prior et al., 2020.

claim: Single-point mutations at one of three hotspot positions (G12, G13, and Q61) in KRAS result in six possible substitutions that inhibit the intrinsic or extrinsic GTPase activity of the protein.
source: single-point mutations at one of three hotpot positions (G12, G13, and Q61) result in six possible substitutions that inhibit the intrinsic or extrinsic GTPase activity of the protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS mutations.

claim: KRAS mutations render KRAS constitutively GTP-bound and active, which is oncogenic.
source: These mutations render KRAS constitutively GTP-bound and active, which is well known to be oncogenic (Simanshu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simanshu et al., 2017.

claim: The most common oncogenic KRAS mutation is G12C in non-small cell lung cancer.
source: For example, the most common oncogenic KRAS mutation is G12C in non-small cell lung cancer
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prior et al., 2020.

claim: The most common oncogenic KRAS mutation is Q61H in plasma cell myeloma.
source: but Q61H in plasma cell myeloma (Prior et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prior et al., 2020.

claim: Mice exhibit a bias of specific oncogenic Kras mutations towards different cancer types.
source: Mice similarly exhibit a bias of specific oncogenic Kras mutations towards different cancer types as different mutant Kras alleles have different tumorigenic potential when activated in different tissues (Li et al., 2018; Poulin et al., 2019; Winters et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2020; Zafra et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different oncogenic mutations affect the ability of Nras to induce tumorigenesis in mice.
source: Different oncogenic mutations also affect the ability of Nras to induce tumorigenesis in mice, as do the same mutations in different RAS isoforms (Burd et al., 2014; Haigis et al., 2008; Kong et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The tissue 'tropism' of cancers towards specific RAS mutations has been appreciated for decades.
source: While this tissue 'tropism' of cancers towards specific RAS mutations has been appreciated for decades (Bos, 1989), the underlying mechanism is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bos, 1989.

claim: Different KRAS mutations can exhibit different degrees of activation (GTP-loading) and/or different sensitivities to positive (RasGEFs) or negative (RasGAPs) regulators.
source: In terms of quantitative signaling, different mutations can exhibit different degrees of activation (GTP-loading) and/or different sensitivities to positive (Ras GTP exchange factors [RasGEFs]) or negative (RAS GTPase activating proteins [RasGAPs]) regulators (Gebregiworgis et al., 2021; Munoz-Maldonado et al., 2019; Simanshu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Various methods to manipulate quantitative Kras signaling affect tumorigenesis.
source: Various methods to manipulate quantitative Kras signaling, such as through modulating recombination rates (Singh et al., 2021), homozygous expression of the mutant allele (Wang et al., 2011), changing codon usage to increase protein expression (Pershing et al., 2015), additional pharmacological activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Cicchini et al., 2017), and so forth (Li et al., 2018), all affect tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The G12R mutant of KRAS exhibits reduced PI3Kα binding and PI3K/AKT signaling compared to the G12D mutant.
source: On the other hand, perhaps one of the best examples of qualitative differences in KRAS signaling is the G12R mutant. Unlike the more canonical G12D mutation, the G12R mutant exhibits reduced the RAS effector PI3Kα binding and PI3K/AKT signaling (Hobbs et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hobbs et al., 2020.

claim: Activating an inducible KrasLSL-G12R allele in the pancreas led to fewer early premalignant lesions compared to the KrasLSL-G12D allele.
source: Activating an inducible KrasLSL-G12R allele in the pancreas led to fewer early premalignant lesions compared to the much more tumorigenic KrasLSL-G12D allele (Zafra et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zafra et al., 2020.

claim: KRAS mutations are often initiating, being sufficient to induce tumorigenesis in mice and truncal in many human cancers.
source: KRAS mutations are often initiating, being sufficient to induce tumorigenesis in mice and truncal in many human cancers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS mutations.

claim: The G12D mutation places a negatively-charged headgroup into the catalytic cleft of RAS and blocks extrinsic (RasGAP-mediated) GTPase activity.
source: G12D places a negatively-charged headgroup into the catalytic cleft of RAS and blocks extrinsic (RasGAP-mediated) GTPase activity (Parker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parker et al., 2018.

claim: The Q61R mutation replaces the catalytic amino acid with one that has a positively-charged headgroup, disrupting the position of the active site water molecule necessary for intrinsic GTP hydrolysis.
source: On the other hand, Q61R replaces the catalytic amino acid with one that has a positively-charged headgroup, disrupting the position of the active site water molecule necessary for intrinsic GTP hydrolysis (Buhrman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buhrman et al., 2010.

claim: Q61R has significantly lower GTP exchange and hydrolysis rates than G12D in Nras.
source: Comparing these two mutants directly reveals Q61R to have significantly lower GTP exchange and hydrolysis rates than G12D in Nras (Burd et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burd et al., 2014.

claim: Q61R has reduced RasGAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis rates in Kras compared to G12D.
source: and reduced RasGAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis rates in Kras (Rabara et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rabara et al., 2019.

claim: The G12D mutant of Nras was less oncogenic than Q61R in melanoma.
source: In those few cases in which the tumorigenic potential of the G12D and Q61R mutants of the same Ras isoform has been directly compared in mice, tissue-specific expression of the G12D mutant was less oncogenic than Q61R in both Nras-induced melanoma (Burd et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burd et al., 2014.

claim: The G12D mutant of Kras was less oncogenic than Q61R in myeloproliferative neoplasm.
source: and Kras-induced myeloproliferative neoplasm (Kong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2016.

claim: The first three coding exons of Kras were fused and encoded by either their native rare codons or common codons to alter protein expression.
source: To alter the expression of these two mutants, the first three coding exons of Kras were fused and encoded by either their native rare codons, which is known to retard Kras protein expression, or common codons to increase Kras protein expression (Ali et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018; Lampson et al., 2013; Pershing et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Altering mammalian codon usage modulates protein expression in vivo.
source: We chose the novel approach of altering mammalian codon usage to modulate protein expression in vivo (Li and Counter, 2021; Pershing et al., 2015; Sasine et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each of the four Kras alleles began with an LSL transcriptional/translational repressor sequence (STOP) flanked by loxP sites engineered into the intron of Kras following the first non-coding exon.
source: Each began with an LSL transcriptional/translational repressor sequence (STOP) flanked by loxP sites (Jackson et al., 2001) engineered into the intron of Kras following the first non-coding exon to provide temporal and spatial control of gene expression.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 93 rare codons were converted to their common counterparts in the common codon versions of the alleles.
source: This was followed by a fusion of the first three coding exons encoded by either their native (nat) rare codons, which are known to retard protein expression, or 93 of these rare codons converted to their common (com) counterparts to increase protein expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The remainder of the Kras gene was left intact to generate both Kras4a and Kras4b isoforms.
source: Finally, the remainder of the gene was left intact so as to generate the two Kras4a and Kras4b isoforms, as both contribute to tumorigenesis (To et al., 2008), potentially through unique protein interactions (Amendola et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to To et al., 2008 and Amendola et al., 2019.

claim: All four Kras alleles could be recombined upon the expression of Cre recombinase.
source: and validated that all four alleles could be recombined upon the expression of Cre recombinase (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The four Kras alleles yield a stepwise increase in endogenous Kras activity in the ascending order of KrasnatG12D<KrasnatQ61R<KrascomG12D<KrascomQ61R in MEF cultures.
source: RBD pull-down followed by immunoblot demonstrated the stepwise increase in Kras expression and activity levels in the ascending order of KrasnatG12D<KrasnatQ61R <KrascomG12D<KrascomQ61R in both conditions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Q61R mutant is more active than the G12D mutant.
source: Thus, endogenous expression of these four alleles revealed that the Q61R mutant is more active than the G12D mutant
evidence: This is based on RBD pull-down data from MEF cultures.

claim: Changing rare codons to common increases the expression and activity of endogenous Kras oncoprotein.
source: and changing rare codons to common increases the expression and activity of endogenous Kras oncoprotein.
evidence: This is based on RBD pull-down data from MEF cultures.

claim: A stepwise increase in Kras expression and activity consistent with codon usage and oncogenic mutation was observed in lung tissue in vivo.
source: As in the case of the MEF cultures, we observed a stepwise increase in Kras expression and activity consistent with the codon usage and oncogenic mutation in this allelic set (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B C, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: The expected increase in three Ras target gene transcripts was observed when Kras was encoded with common codons, which was further increased in the Q61R-mutant background.
source: This revealed the expected increase in three such transcripts when Kras was encoded with common codons, which was further increased in the Q61R-mutant background (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B C, Figure 1—source data 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and C.

claim: There was a clear increase in the level of phosphorylated proteins of the MAPK pathway and downstream transcription factors upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele compared to activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele.
source: When normalized to the control tissue, there was a clear increase in the level of phosphorylated proteins of the MAPK pathway and downstream transcription factors upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele compared to activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: There was a stepwise increase in early-onset and tumor burden of pulmonary lesions in lock step with the increased biochemical activity of the oncoproteins in the ascending order of KrasnatG12D<KrasnatQ61R<KrascomG12D<KrascomQ61R.
source: This revealed a stepwise increase in early-onset and tumor burden of pulmonary lesions in lock step with the increased biochemical activity of the oncoproteins in the ascending order of KrasnatG12D<KrasnatQ61R <KrascomG12D<KrascomQ61R (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The G12D-mutant alleles preferentially developed atypical alveolar hyperplasia (AAH), whereas bronchiolar hyperplasia/dysplasia (BH) lesions were more prevalent with the Q61R-mutant alleles.
source: Finally, we find preliminary evidence in a few animals that the G12D-mutant alleles preferentially developed atypical alveolar hyperplasia (AAH), whereas bronchiolar hyperplasia/dysplasia (BH) lesions were more prevalent with the Q61R-mutant alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: 7, 15, 73, and 701 genes were differentially expressed upon activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D, KrasLSL-natQ61R, KrasLSL-comG12D, and KrasLSL-comQ61R alleles, respectively, compared to the wild-type Kras allele.
source: Namely, we identified 7, 15, 73, and 701 genes were differentially expressed (with absolute log2 fold change larger than 2, and adjusted p-value less than 5%) upon activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D, KrasLSL-natQ61R, KrasLSL-comG12D, and KrasLSL-comQ61R alleles, respectively, compared to the wild-type Kras allele (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–6, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–6.

claim: The two native-encoded alleles decreased KRAS Signaling UP hallmarks while the two common-encoded alleles induced signaling events related to oncogenic stress.
source: Comparing the transcriptomes of the two Kras alleles encoded with native rare versus common codons revealed that the two native-encoded alleles decreased KRAS Signaling UP hallmarks while the two common-encoded alleles induced signaling events related to oncogenic stress, such as an increase in Oxidative Phosphorylation, Glycolysis, Reactive Oxygen Species, MTORC1 signaling, Peroxisome, Xenobiotic Metabolism, and UV Response UP hallmarks and a decrease in UV Response DN, Hedgehog Signaling, and Apical Junction hallmarks (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both G12D-mutant alleles induced the Estrogen Response Late hallmark while the Q61R-mutant alleles induced DNA Repair and P53 Pathway and decreased Interferon Alpha Response hallmarks.
source: Comparing the G12D versus Q61R transcriptomes revealed both G12D-mutant alleles induced the Estrogen Response Late hallmark while the Q61R-mutant alleles induced DNA Repair and P53 Pathway and decreased Interferon Alpha Response hallmarks, suggesting that there is a strong tumor-suppressive response uniquely activated by the Q61R-mutant alleles (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D allele resulted in transcriptional signatures suggestive of an expansion of multipotent cells.
source: Activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D allele resulted in transcriptional signatures suggestive of an expansion of multipotent cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A and B.

claim: Activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele had all features of a potent oncogenic signaling leading to hyperproliferation and oncogenic-induced stress.
source: Conversely, activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele had all features of a potent oncogenic signaling leading to hyperproliferation and oncogenic-induced stress.
evidence: This is based on GSEA hallmarks from transcriptome analysis.

claim: The level of protein/phosphoproteins of RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, Growth, DNA repair, senescence/autophagy/apoptosis, and IL/Jak/Stat pathways was higher upon activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R compared to the KrasLSL-natG12D allele.
source: This revealed that the level of protein/phosphoproteins of RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, Growth, DNA repair, senescence/autophagy/apoptosis, and IL/Jak/Stat pathways was higher upon activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R compared to the KrasLSL-natG12D allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 9 and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: The median life span of mice progressively increased from 14 days upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele to 150 days upon activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele.
source: Plotting the percent survival for each of the four genotypes by the Kaplan–Meier approach revealed that the median life span of mice progressively increased from 14 days upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele to 150 days upon activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Median survivals were statistically different, except between the KrasLSL-natG12D/+ versus KrasLSL-natQ61R/+ cohorts.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed that median survivals were statistically different, except between the KrasLSL-natG12D/+ versus KrasLSL-natQ61R/+ cohorts (Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Median survival was significantly decreased in mice when Kras was encoded with common compared to native rare codons.
source: Of note, median survival was significantly decreased in mice with when Kras was encoded with common compared to native rare codons.
evidence: This is based on Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.

claim: Survival was decreased in the mice with the Q61R compared to the G12D mutation when the allele contained the same codon usage.
source: Survival was also decreased in the mice with the Q61R compared to the G12D mutation when the allele contained the same codon usage (KrasLSL-natQ61R versus KrasLSL-natG12D and KrasLSL-comQ61R versus Kras LSL-comG12D).
evidence: This is based on Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.

claim: The level of active oncoprotein is the dominant determinant of cancer survival in this model.
source: As both common codons and the Q61R mutation increase Kras activity, we suggest that the level of active oncoprotein is the dominant determinant of cancer survival in this model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival data and Kras activity measurements.

claim: The incidence of hematolymphopoietic neoplasias increased with the biochemical activity of the Kras oncoprotein.
source: The incidence of hematolymphopoietic neoplasias increased with the biochemical activity of the Kras oncoprotein, as determined from analysis of MEF cultures and lung tissue.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis of spleen and thymus from the global activation study.

claim: Most of the KrasLSL-natG12D mice after tamoxifen injection had no evidence of hematolymphopoietic neoplasms, although some mice had pathological features consistent with malignant lymphoma.
source: Beginning with the least active oncoprotein, most of the KrasLSL-natG12D mice after tamoxifen injection had no evidence of hematolymphopoietic neoplasms, although some mice had pathological features consistent with malignant lymphoma.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis.

claim: The incidence of malignant lymphoma increased with KrasLSL-natQ61R allele, and then again upon activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele.
source: The incidence of malignant lymphoma increased with KrasLSL-natQ61R allele, and then again upon activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele induced severe myeloproliferative disease (MPD) with 100% penetrance.
source: Lastly, activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele induced severe myeloproliferative disease (MPD) with 100% penetrance, with extensive myeloproliferative infiltrates throughout many tissues (Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 4 and 5, and not shown).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B, C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Proliferative lesions of forestomach and oral squamous epithelium were preferentially induced by the oncogenic G12D mutant of Kras encoded by either native or common codons.
source: Proliferative lesions of forestomach and oral squamous epithelium were preferentially induced by the oncogenic G12D mutant of Kras encoded by either native or common codons.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis of forestomach and oral tissues.

claim: Activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced squamous hyperplasia as well as mild and moderate grades of 'atypical' or dysplastic squamous lesions in the forestomach mucosa.
source: In the case of the forestomach tumors, pathological analysis performed as above revealed that activation of the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced squamous hyperplasia as well as mild and moderate grades of 'atypical' or dysplastic squamous lesions in the forestomach mucosa.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis.

claim: No squamous proliferative changes were detected upon activating the KrasLSL-natQ61R allele in the forestomach.
source: Conversely, we did not detect any squamous proliferative changes upon activating the KrasLSL-natQ61R allele (Figure 4B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, and Supplementary files 4 and 5)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele induced more severe grades of forestomach squamous lesions while activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele induced lesions that were of moderate grades.
source: Specifically, activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele induced more severe grades of forestomach squamous lesions while activation of the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele now induced lesions that were of moderate grades (Figure 4B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced minimal to mild grade squamous lesions in the oral cavity, while activating the KrasLSL-natQ61R allele was not tumorigenic.
source: Similar analysis of oral tumors revealed that activating the KrasLSL-natG12D allele induced minimal to mild grade squamous lesions, while activating the KrasLSL-natQ61R allele was not tumorigenic.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis.

claim: Activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele induced severe squamous papilloma in all mice in the oral cavity, while activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele induced a mixture of moderate and severe grade squamous papillomas.
source: Namely, activating the KrasLSL-comG12D allele induced severe squamous papilloma in all mice, while activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R allele induced a mixture of moderate and severe grade squamous papillomas (Figure 4B and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The G12D mutation consistently induced more AAH and/or adenomas than the Q61R mutation when Kras was encoded with either common or native rare codons in the lung.
source: Pathological analysis performed as above in the lung revealed that the G12D mutation consistently induced more AAH and/or adenomas than the Q61R mutation when Kras was encoded with either common or native rare codons, both in terms of the number of animals with these lesions and the total number of these lesions per animal (Figure 4B and F, Figure 4—figure supplements 5; 6A, and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and F, and Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6A.

claim: Converting rare codons to common amplified the severity of lung lesions detected, which was particularly evident in the confluence of large peripheral AAH lesions induced preferentially by the KrasLSL-comG12D allele.
source: As was the case with forestomach and oral lesions, converting rare codons to common amplified the severity of lesions detected, which was particularly evident in the confluence of large peripheral AAH lesions induced preferentially by theKrasLSL-comG12D allele (Figure 4B and F, Figure 4—figure supplements 5; 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and F, and Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6B.

claim: No BH lesions were induced by either mutant when Kras was encoded with native rare codons and instead were only prevalent when Kras was encoded with common codons.
source: However, no BH lesions were induced by either mutant when Kras was encoded with native rare codons and instead were only prevalent when Kras was encoded with common codons.
evidence: This is based on pathological analysis.

claim: The number of animals with BH lesions was higher upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R compared to the KrasLSL-comG12D allele.
source: Further, the number of animals with BH lesions was higher upon activating the KrasLSL-comQ61R compared to the KrasLSL-comG12D allele (Figure 4—figure supplements 5; 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6C.

claim: No overt proliferative lesions were detected at necropsy or by histopathological analysis in the pancreas, kidney, or liver.
source: Despite widespread tumorigenesis, we note that no overt proliferative lesions were detected at necropsy or by histopathological analysis in the pancreas, kidney, or liver (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Many organs appear to be intrinsically resistant to the tumorigenic effects of oncogenic Kras, regardless of the mutation type or expression levels tested.
source: Thus, many organs appear to be intrinsically resistant to the tumorigenic effects of oncogenic Kras, regardless of the mutation type or expression levels tested, at least within the time frame of this study and in the tested Rosa26CreERT2/+ background.
evidence: This is based on the absence of tumors in multiple organs despite global activation of the alleles.

claim: Tissues differ in their sensitivities to quantitative and/or qualitative RAS signaling, both as a product of oncoprotein signaling and the cellular response thereof.
source: Here, we describe the effect of activating four inducible oncogenic Kras alleles encoding two very different mutants in a native rare versus common codon background to explore the mechanisms underlying the bias of specific oncogenic KRAS mutations towards distinct cancer types. We suggest that the unique tumor patterns arising from each of these mutant alleles implies that tissues differ in their sensitivities to quantitative and/or qualitative RAS signaling, both as a product of oncoprotein signaling and the cellular response thereof.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data of the study.

claim: The four alleles were generated by fusing the first three coding exons, an artificial gene architecture.
source: First, these four alleles were generated by fusing the first three coding exons, an artificial gene architecture, and hence can only be compared to themselves and not to other types of Kras alleles.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors.

claim: These alleles were induced by an injection of tamoxifen to activate CreER expressed from the Rosa26 locus.
source: Second, these alleles were induced by an injection of tamoxifen to activate CreER expressed from the Rosa26 locus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Kras activity of this allelic set was defined in MEFs and lung tissue.
source: Third, Kras activity of this allelic set was defined in MEFs and lung tissue.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Cell-type differences in regulatory feedback pathways or codon-dependent expression could result in different levels of Kras expression, activation, or signaling compared to that observed in MEF cultures and lung tissue.
source: We therefore acknowledge that cell-type differences in regulatory feedback pathways (Lake et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018) or codon-dependent expression (Peterson et al., 2020) could result in different levels of Kras expression, activation, or signaling compared to that observed in MEF cultures and lung tissue, which were used to define the activity of each Kras oncoprotein.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: By the nature of the experimental design, tissue types with slower tumor progression are underrepresented.
source: Fourth, by the nature of the experimental design, tissue types with slower tumor progression are underrepresented, and hence may respond differently to activation of the different Kras alleles when assessed more specifically.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors.

claim: EMT is known to promote stem cell-like fates.
source: EMT is known to promote stem cell-like fates (Floor et al., 2011; Mani et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Floor et al., 2011 and Mani et al., 2008.

claim: Activation of oncogenic Kras in the murine lung generates tumors with many tissue lineages.
source: and activation of oncogenic Kras in the murine lung generates tumors with many tissue lineages (Tata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tata et al., 2018.

claim: Single-cell transcriptome profiling of lung tumors induced by targeted delivery of AAV-Cre in an KrasLSL-G12D/+;Trp53fl/fl background identified a distinct population with a mixed cellular identity.
source: In support, single-cell transcriptome profiling of lung tumors induced by targeted delivery of AAV-Cre in an KrasLSL-G12D/+;Trp53fl/fl background identified a distinct population with a mixed cellular identity (Marjanovic et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marjanovic et al., 2020.

claim: Globally activating a 'super-rare' version of KrasLSL-rareG12D allele encoded by the rarest codons induced hematolymphopoietic neoplasias, although in a much-protracted time frame.
source: To independently validate this result, we found that globally activating a 'super-rare' version of KrasLSL-rareG12D allele encoded by the rarest codons induced hematolymphopoietic neoplasias, although in a much-protracted time frame (Figure 4—figure supplement 7 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: GEF-mediated GTP exchange is more rapid with a Q61L versus G12V mutant of Kras.
source: In support, GEF-mediated GTP exchange is more rapid with a Q61L versus G12V mutant of Kras (Smith et al., 2013)
